subject: Biology
title: Why Do We Get Goosebumps?
summary: A tiny muscle at the base of each hair, the arrector pili, contracts in cold or fear: the hair stands up and the skin around it rises into a bump.
keyPoints: Each hair follicle has a tiny smooth muscle, the **arrector pili**.
Cold or strong emotion fires **sympathetic nerves** and releases **adrenaline**; the muscle contracts involuntarily.
The hair stands upright and the skin around it bunches into a bump: a **goosebump**.

In furry animals raised fur traps air (insulation) and makes them look bigger; in humans it is mostly a leftover reflex, though the same nerve-muscle pair helps hair regrow in long cold (research, 2020).

list: Trigger: cold, fear, or a strong emotion (even music).
Sympathetic nerves fire and adrenaline is released.
The arrector pili (smooth, involuntary muscle) contracts.
It pulls the slanted follicle upright: the hair stands, the skin above rises into a bump.

head: Effect
Benefit
rows: Raised fur traps a thicker air layer

blocks.p: Humans have too little body hair for either effect, so the reflex is largely a leftover from furry ancestors.

quiz.q: The muscle that causes goosebumps is the:
quiz.explain: A tiny smooth muscle attached to each hair follicle.

quiz.q: For a furry animal in the cold, raised fur:
options: Traps a layer of insulating air
quiz.explain: The air layer slows heat loss.

quiz.q: Why do goosebumps barely warm humans?
options: We have too little body hair
quiz.explain: Sparse hair cannot trap much air.
